citizen.name: capable
citizen.line: Able to start a community that lasts, and to be a good member of one.

traits.name: Sovereign
traits.grant: You can leave with your name, your connections and your work.

traits.name: Civil
traits.grant: You can disagree with a stranger without making an enemy.

traits.name: Mobile
traits.grant: You choose your communities on purpose, and let others choose theirs.

traits.name: Enduring
traits.grant: You know why communities die, and what the lasting ones share.

lessons.title: Own Your Exit
lessons.promise: Why cheap leaving keeps a place fair, and how to own what you'd take with you.

cards.text: A restaurant can keep a dress code because you can walk across the street. *House rules stay fair when leaving is cheap.*
On most apps your name, your followers and your posts live inside the app. Leaving means starting from zero, so its house rules start to work like laws.
So own the parts yourself: your name, your connections, your work. Some open networks are built that way, and there an app is just one front door among many.
*A name you control.* An email address on your own domain survives any change of provider. Some social networks let that domain be your handle too.
*Keys you can take back.* Give each app a limited key, never your password, like a valet key that won't open the trunk. Big accounts list the ones you've given.
*Connections and work you sign.* On some open networks every post and follow carries your signature, so any app can show it and anyone can check it.

cards.def: Being able to take the data you gave a service to another one, in a format it can read. In the EU it has been a legal right since 2018 (GDPR, Article 20).

cards.heading: Keeping your number, 2003
cards.text: In 1996 US regulators ordered mobile carriers to let customers keep their numbers when they switched, starting in 1999. The industry called it too costly and won delays. The regulators' reasoning was plain: people stay with a carrier they dislike when leaving costs them their number. A court turned down the carriers' challenge, and in November 2003 numbers began to move. Within a year, more than 8.5 million had.

cards.claim: In 1970 the economist Albert Hirschman, who wrote the classic book on exit, saw a catch: when leaving is too easy, people stop speaking up. Why argue about the dress code when you can cross the street? Then problems go unfixed.
cards.reply: True, and he wrote the other half too: the possibility of exit makes voice work better. Complaints get answered when everyone knows you could go. You don't have to leave the biggest app to keep it in check. It only has to know you can.

cards.text: If the app you use most changed its rules tomorrow, what could you take with you, and what would you leave behind?

cards.prompt: Own one piece of your digital life this week: your name, your connections or your work. Start with the one you'd miss most.
steps: Export it into a folder you control, then open the file to check it's all there.
Open your account settings and take back the keys of apps you no longer use.
Find a login only one company can recover, and add a backup way in that you control.
Trying a run-it-yourself guide? Use a test account, and never paste a recovery phrase anywhere.

sources.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
sources.author: Albert O. Hirschman
sources.note: The classic account of leaving versus speaking up. Easy exit can weaken the habit of voice, yet the possibility of exit makes voice work better.

sources.title: Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media
sources.author: Martin Kleppmann, Paul Frazee, Jay Graber and others
sources.note: How one open network lets you claim a domain you own as your handle, signs every change to your data, and lets you move hosts without losing your followers.

sources.title: Cellular Telecommunications & Internet Association v. FCC
sources.author: US Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit
sources.note: The ruling that let mobile number portability start in November 2003. It quotes the regulator's reasoning: people stay with carriers they dislike when leaving costs them their number.

sources.title: 8.5M customers switch during first year of LNP
sources.author: RCR Wireless News
sources.note: A trade report of the regulator's count after portability's first year: more than 8.5 million people took a phone number to a new carrier.

sources.title: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 20: Right to data portability
sources.author: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
sources.note: The EU law, applied since 25 May 2018, that lets you get the data you gave a service in a machine-readable format and move it to another.

work.caption: A guide to running your own node and the app that reads from it, start to finish.
An app plus a tutorial for running everything yourself.
A full-featured app that reads from a node you run.
Your own node and a command-line app, set up in a few commands or by a coding agent.

lessons.title: Where Manners Come From
lessons.promise: How manners grew out of power, and why they let strangers count on each other.

cards.text: For centuries, courtesy guides told diners not to blow their noses on the tablecloth. In 1939 the sociologist Norbert Elias turned such books into a history of manners.
Why did manners change? Not because people simply got nicer, Elias said. As a few states won a monopoly on violence, armed nobles had to become courtiers.
At court one outburst could cost you everything. Control that began in the ruler's guards and favor moved inside you: *self-restraint*, taught to children until it felt like nature.

cards.heading: A handbook for boys, 1530
cards.text: In 1530 Erasmus wrote a short Latin handbook on how a boy should behave among adults. It was translated into many languages, and the French typeface used to print one translation came to be called *civilité*. Erasmus still wrote openly about the body. Later manners books stopped mentioning such things at all. The feelings themselves had made them unmentionable.

cards.def: The links by which you depend on many strangers for food, goods and safety. As they lengthened, court restraint spread with them: long chains reward people who behave predictably.

cards.text: Is Singapore orderly because people are polite, or because the rules are enforced? Read through Elias, it's a false choice: enforcement came first, then politeness carried much of the load.
Arguing with a stranger? Say their point back until they'd sign it. Argue with the point and keep the person out of it. Leave them a way to come around.
Elias's book appeared in 1939. In 1942 his mother was deported to Theresienstadt and murdered at Treblinka. The restraint he traced was never a guarantee.

cards.claim: Who decides what counts as civil? In Elias's story it was the ruler and his court. Give one group the power to define and punish incivility, under rules it can rewrite, and the moderator becomes the king, with every reason to call dissent rudeness.
cards.reply: Elias has no easy answer: his courts were not free places. But a moderator you can walk away from, with your name and your work, is weaker than a king. Before you join a community, find out who writes its rules and how you can appeal.

cards.text: In the places you trust most, which came first: the manners, or someone willing to enforce them?

cards.prompt: This week, disagree once with someone you don't know well, without making an enemy.
steps: Pick one manners rule you follow without thinking. What does it let strangers count on?
Choose something small, and say their point back before you answer it.
If you feel the heat rising, wait an hour before you reply.
Afterward, note what kept you civil: your own restraint, or a rule someone enforces?

sources.title: The Civilizing Process: Sociogenetic and Psychogenetic Investigations
sources.author: Norbert Elias
sources.note: Published in German in Basel in 1939; in English in two volumes (1978, 1982), one volume 1994, revised 2000. Manners books read alongside the rise of states.

sources.title: The Rise of the Fork
sources.author: Keith Thomas
sources.note: A review of the first English volume. Thomas sums up the thesis, that refinement grew as chains of dependence lengthened, and faults the book as ethnocentric.

sources.title: Civilité
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: The typeface Robert Granjon cut in 1557, named after early books printed in it, including a 1559 French translation of Erasmus's handbook.

work.caption: Where does a society's predictability come from: politeness, or enforcement?
How everyday civility builds the trust that cooperation runs on.

lessons.title: Vote With Your Feet
lessons.promise: Why choosing where you belong is a vote, and how to make that choice on purpose.

cards.text: Most people vote with their feet without calling it that. Muting a group chat, quitting a job, moving across town: each says something about what a person wants.
Parks, police and flood walls have no price tag. Once built, they serve everyone nearby, so nobody says what they're worth. How does a town learn what people want?
In 1956 the economist Charles Tiebout answered: a country has many towns, each with its own bundle of taxes and services. People who can move pick the bundle that fits.

cards.heading: Three towns, three bundles
cards.text: Picture three towns. One taxes high and runs strong schools and big parks. One taxes low and leaves you alone. One sits in between. A family with young children picks the first. A retired couple on a fixed income picks the second. Nobody fills in a survey: *the move is the answer*. Each town watches who arrives and who leaves, and competes to be chosen.

cards.def: What happens when people who can move choose among many communities: each one fills with people who want roughly what it offers.

cards.heading: Fewer people move now
cards.text: In 1948, 20.2 percent of people in the US had moved in the past year, by the Census Bureau's count. In 2021 it was 8.4 percent, the lowest on record. Jobs, house prices and family hold people in place, and Tiebout's model set them aside: his residents lived on dividends. Online comes closer, if your name and connections come with you: switching takes a minute and your job stays put.
Sorting works only if communities differ. One that bores you may suit someone else perfectly. Look before you settle, *choose on purpose*, and let others choose differently.

cards.claim: Sorting can harden inequality: people sort by money as well as taste, and rich towns zone others out. And Albert Hirschman argued in 1970 that easy exit can drain a group of its most demanding members, the ones best able to fix it.
cards.reply: Both are real. Defenders keep choice for local things and fund fairness, such as welfare, at the state or national level; critics doubt that's enough. Hirschman's own remedy is loyalty: staying long enough to speak. Leaving tells a community something is wrong. Only your voice tells it what.

cards.prompt: Pick one community you belong to, online or off, and read it the way Tiebout would: as a bundle you chose, or drifted into.
steps: List what it asks of you: money, time, attention, rules.
List what it gives back: people, skills, safety, fun.
Before you leave anything, say once, plainly, what you would change.
Name a community you would never join that clearly works for its members.

sources.title: A Pure Theory of Local Expenditures
sources.author: Charles M. Tiebout
sources.note: The short paper behind this lesson: many towns, mobile residents, and the choice of where to live revealing what people want. He calls his model extreme, and says why.

sources.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
sources.author: Albert O. Hirschman
sources.note: The classic case that leaving and speaking up do different jobs, and that easy exit can quietly drain a community of its best critics.

sources.title: Pandemic Did Not Disrupt Decline in Rate of People Moving
sources.author: Kristin Kerns-D'Amore, Joey Marshall and Brian McKenzie, US Census Bureau
sources.note: The Census Bureau's account of the long fall in how often people in the US move, from 20.2 percent in 1948 to 8.4 percent in 2021.

lessons.title: What Lasts
lessons.promise: What the communes that lasted had in common, and why good intentions were not enough.

cards.text: Around 1874 the journalist Charles Nordhoff toured America's communes, from Maine to Kentucky to Oregon. For each, he recorded how it was governed, what it made and what it believed.
The ones that lasted shared a short list: a creed that mattered to members, leaders with real authority who lived like everyone else, steady work, plain living, and no debt.
People assumed a commune would die with its founder. Nordhoff found most had already outlived theirs. The Harmonists carried on after George Rapp died in 1847.

cards.heading: One town, two experiments
cards.text: In 1824 George Rapp's Harmonists decided to sell their Indiana town and move back east. In 1825 the reformer Robert Owen bought it. Owen renamed it New Harmony and appealed to the public. About a thousand people came. Many could not do the work, farms and workshops sat idle, and people argued over how to govern. It had broken up by 1827. Rapp's society lasted from 1805 to 1905.

cards.heading: Why Bishop Hill fell
cards.text: In 1846 Swedish settlers led by the preacher Eric Janson began arriving at Bishop Hill, Illinois. By 1848 there were about eight hundred. In 1850 Janson was shot in the county courthouse. Nordhoff's diagnosis was mostly money and structure: debt and lawsuits, trustees who reported irregularly, no one with the power to change course, and young people who found the life dull. By 1862 the property was divided.

cards.def: A trial stage for newcomers. Shaker applicants went first to a novitiate family; at Zoar, probationary members kept their property until they joined fully. Joining took time.

cards.text: Lesson 1 said cheap exit keeps places fair. The Harmonists made exit costly: after 1836, anyone who quit had no claim to what they'd brought. Choose openly which you want.

cards.claim: Nordhoff mostly toured survivors. Groups that collapsed in a year left no village to visit, and may have shared the same traits. And lasting had a price: the Shakers and Harmonists endured while giving up marriage and children, and slowly emptied.
cards.reply: Partly fair. Nordhoff did study a failure, Bishop Hill. In 1972 the sociologist Rosabeth Moss Kanter compared communes that lasted 25 years or more with those that did not, and stronger commitment predicted longer life. Still, endurance shows a design works, not that it is worth living in.

cards.text: Nordhoff called communal life “not amateur work”. If you started a group this year, what would keep it going once your enthusiasm ran out?

cards.prompt: Pick a group you run, help run, or want to start. Hold it up to Nordhoff's list.
steps: Write its bond in one sentence. Would members write the same one?
Check the money: does it owe anything, or rest on one person paying?
Name who could run it for a month if you stepped away.
Decide what joining should ask of newcomers, and tell them what leaving will cost.

sources.title: The Communistic Societies of the United States
sources.author: Charles Nordhoff
sources.note: A journalist's first-hand survey of the Shakers, Harmonists, Zoar, Amana, Oneida and others. Communistic here means voluntary groups holding property in common. Free to read.

sources.title: Commitment and Community: Communes and Utopias in Sociological Perspective
sources.author: Rosabeth Moss Kanter
sources.note: A sociologist's answer to survivorship bias: 19th-century communes that lasted compared with those that did not, and the commitment mechanisms that set the survivors apart.

lessons.title: Know Who Came First
lessons.promise: Why places keep their first settlers' habits for centuries, and how to read them.

cards.text: When was America founded? In his 1989 book *Albion's Seed*, the historian David Hackett Fischer answers: four times, by four groups from different corners of Britain.
Each group brought its folkways: how to speak, build, marry, worship, raise children and settle quarrels. Fischer argues those habits outlived the settlers and still mark American regions.
Each also brought its own idea of freedom. Fischer names four: ordered, hegemonic, reciprocal and natural liberty. Americans still argue about freedom in all four accents.

cards.heading: Four waves, four places
cards.text: From 1629 to 1640, Puritan families from East Anglia came to Massachusetts. From the 1640s, royalist gentry and their servants from southern England came to Virginia. From 1675, Quakers from the North Midlands settled the Delaware Valley. From 1718 to 1775, families from the borders of England and Scotland, and from Ulster, moved into the Appalachian backcountry.

cards.heading: Four ideas of freedom
cards.text: In Massachusetts, liberty meant a town's freedom to order itself, and each member's duty to that order. In Virginia it meant the power to rule others, held by a few. The Quakers of William Penn's colony, granted in 1681, offered freedom of worship to others because they claimed it for themselves. In the backcountry, liberty meant being left alone and settling things yourself.

cards.def: The geographer Wilbur Zelinsky's 1973 idea: the first group to build a working society in a place sets its culture. Later, larger waves of newcomers mostly adapt to it.

cards.text: This cuts both ways for you. Joining a group means joining habits set long before you came. Starting one means *your first habits* may outlast you.

cards.claim: Four British groups cannot explain America. Fischer says little about the Dutch, the Germans, Native nations, or the Africans brought in chains, and he may understate how much the new land changed the settlers.
cards.reply: Much of this is fair, and historians said so in a 1991 journal symposium on the book. Fischer meant it as a first volume; *African Founders* followed in 2022. What stays open is how strongly first habits persist, not whether they do.

cards.text: Think of a group you belong to. Who founded it, and which of their habits do you follow without ever having chosen them?

cards.prompt: Read one community you belong to, or are about to join, for its founding folkways.
steps: Find out who started it and what they cared about most.
List three habits newcomers absorb without ever being told.
Ask what freedom means there: order, rank, conscience, or being left alone?
If you are starting something, write down the first habits you want to last.

sources.title: Albion's Seed: Four British Folkways in America
sources.author: David Hackett Fischer
sources.note: The book behind this lesson: four migrations from Britain, the folkways each carried, and the four ideas of liberty they left. Long, but each part stands alone.

sources.title: The Cultural Geography of the United States
sources.author: Wilbur Zelinsky
sources.note: A geographer's survey of American culture regions, and the source of the idea that a place's first effective settlers set its lasting character.

sources.title: Albion's Seed: Four British Folkways in America, A Symposium
sources.author: The William and Mary Quarterly, vol. 48
sources.note: Historians of early America test the book's claims, region by region, and Fischer replies. The best place to see where the argument is strong and where it is thin.
